title: Rupesh Patel
text:
My name is Rupesh Patel. I moved from Toronto, Ontario, to Vancouver to study in the Master of Data Science program at UBC.
I have a bachelor’s degree in Mechanical Engineering and previously worked as a data engineer. Through this program, I hope to build my understanding of statistics, data science, and machine learning.
After completing the program, I plan to work as a data scientist. This website shares my background, experiences in MDS, and small data analysis projects using Python and R.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
In this post, I use R and Python together to compare fuel efficiency between automatic and manual cars.
I prepare the data in R, calculate group summaries in Python, and bring the results back into R to create a table and plot. The reticulate package allows the two languages to share objects without saving intermediate CSV files.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
In this post, I use R and Python together to compare fuel efficiency between automatic and manual cars.
I prepare the data in R, calculate group summaries in Python, and bring the results back into R to create a table and plot. The reticulate package allows the two languages to share objects without saving intermediate CSV files.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Data source
I use the built-in R dataset mtcars: Motor Trend Car Road Tests.
The data was extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend magazine and contains 32 cars from the 1973–74 model years. The R documentation cites Henderson and Velleman (1981).
The dataset comes with R, so no separate download is needed.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Set up R and Python

library(reticulate)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

use_virtualenv("../../.venv", required = TRUE)

py_config()

This post is inside posts/r-and-python, so ../../.venv points to the Python environment at the repository root. This relative path also works when the repository is cloned into a different location.
The configuration output shows which Python interpreter is being used.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Prepare the data in R
I select fuel efficiency, weight, and transmission type. The original transmission variable uses 0 for automatic and 1 for manual, so I create readable labels.

cars_bonus <- mtcars |>
  select(mpg, wt, am) |>
  mutate(
    transmission = if_else(am == 0, "Automatic", "Manual")
  )

head(cars_bonus)

                   mpg    wt am transmission
Mazda RX4         21.0 2.620  1       Manual
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0 2.875  1       Manual
Datsun 710        22.8 2.320  1       Manual
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4 3.215  0    Automatic
Hornet Sportabout 18.7 3.440  0    Automatic
Valiant           18.1 3.460  0    Automatic

colSums(is.na(cars_bonus))

         mpg           wt           am transmission 
           0            0            0            0 


There are no missing values in these selected columns. Fuel efficiency is measured in miles per US gallon, and weight is measured in thousands of pounds.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
section: Pass the R data to Python
text:
Pass the R data to Python
In a Python chunk, r.cars_bonus accesses the object created in R. Reticulate converts the R data frame into a pandas DataFrame.

import pandas as pd

cars_python = r.cars_bonus.copy()

print(type(cars_python))

<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>

print("Number of cars:", len(cars_python))

Number of cars: 32

print(cars_python.head())

                    mpg     wt   am transmission
Mazda RX4          21.0  2.620  1.0       Manual
Mazda RX4 Wag      21.0  2.875  1.0       Manual
Datsun 710         22.8  2.320  1.0       Manual
Hornet 4 Drive     21.4  3.215  0.0    Automatic
Hornet Sportabout  18.7  3.440  0.0    Automatic


This confirms that Python received the data prepared in R.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Calculate the summaries in Python
I group the cars by transmission type and calculate the number of cars, average fuel efficiency, and average weight.

transmission_summary = (
    cars_python
    .groupby("transmission", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        number_of_cars=("mpg", "size"),
        average_mpg=("mpg", "mean"),
        average_weight=("wt", "mean")
    )
)

print(transmission_summary.round(2).to_string(index=False))

transmission  number_of_cars  average_mpg  average_weight
   Automatic              19        17.15            3.77
      Manual              13        24.39            2.41


The manual group has an average fuel efficiency of about 24.4 MPG, compared with 17.1 MPG for the automatic group.
However, the manual cars are also lighter on average. Their average weight is about 2.41 thousand pounds, compared with 3.77 thousand pounds for the automatic cars.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
section: Bring the Python results back to R
text:
Bring the Python results back to R
In an R chunk, py$transmission_summary accesses the summary created in Python. I store it as an R object and display it as a table.

summary_r <- py$transmission_summary

knitr::kable(
  summary_r,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Transmission",
    "Number of cars",
    "Average MPG",
    "Average weight (1,000 pounds)"
  )
)










Transmission
Number of cars
Average MPG
Average weight (1,000 pounds)




Automatic
19
17.15
3.77


Manual
13
24.39
2.41





The numbers in this table were calculated in Python and then passed back to R.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Plot the results in R

ggplot(
  summary_r,
  aes(x = transmission, y = average_mpg, fill = transmission)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(average_mpg, 1)),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Automatic" = "#4477AA", "Manual" = "#228833")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average fuel efficiency by transmission",
    x = "Transmission",
    y = "Average fuel efficiency (miles per US gallon)"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Average fuel efficiency by transmission type. The averages were calculated in Python and plotted in R.

title: Comparing fuel efficiency using R and Python
text:
Conclusion
Manual cars have higher average MPG in this dataset, but they are also lighter on average. This comparison does not show that changing the transmission alone would improve fuel efficiency.
The dataset contains only 32 older cars, so these results should not be assumed to describe modern vehicles.
This post demonstrates a shared workflow: R prepares the data, Python calculates the summaries, and R displays the results. The objects are passed between the languages using reticulate.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
I drove into Vancouver on August 9th with a car full of boxes and spent the month before classes on logistics. Orientation was mostly a blur of names, but one thing landed: this is a cohort program — same people, same four courses, same room, every day until May. Then classes started and it was DSCI 551, 523, 511, and 521 all at once, each with labs. The site you are reading is a 521 deliverable, which is a slightly strange thing to write in a blog post.
I assumed the tooling would be the easy part. Instead my first real fight of the term was with SSH: I could not clone from github.ubc.ca at all, and the cause turned out to be an IdentityFile mismatch once I had more than one key on the machine. R surprised me too. I write Python for a living and figured a second language would be translation work, then lost an embarrassing stretch of time to the difference between list(values) and as.list(values), which are not the same thing and do not fail loudly when you pick wrong.
The best surprise was conceptual. In 551 something clicked about the difference between a parametric family, a specific distribution inside it, the parameters that pick it out, and the values you actually observe — four things I had been using interchangeably for years. That is the whole reason I came: I was good at building pipelines and much shakier on what the numbers coming out of them meant. Being the least informed person in the room again is uncomfortable and clearly the point. Ask me again after midterms.



Orientation day on campus.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Do heavier cars tend to have lower fuel efficiency? In this post, I explore the relationship between car weight and miles per gallon. I also compare average fuel efficiency across cylinder groups.
A higher miles-per-gallon value means the car can travel farther using the same amount of fuel.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Data source
I use the built-in R dataset mtcars: Motor Trend Car Road Tests.
The data was extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend magazine and contains 32 cars from the 1973–74 model years. The R documentation cites Henderson and Velleman (1981).
I use the copy included with R, so no separate data download is needed.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Set up

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The setup chunk suppresses package startup messages and warnings to keep the page easier to read.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Explore the data
I select the columns needed for this analysis and check for missing values.

cars <- mtcars |>
  select(mpg, wt, cyl)

head(cars)

                   mpg    wt cyl
Mazda RX4         21.0 2.620   6
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0 2.875   6
Datsun 710        22.8 2.320   4
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4 3.215   6
Hornet Sportabout 18.7 3.440   8
Valiant           18.1 3.460   6

nrow(cars)

[1] 32

colSums(is.na(cars))

mpg  wt cyl 
  0   0   0 


There are 32 cars and no missing values in these three columns. The variables are:

mpg: miles per US gallon.
wt: car weight in thousands of pounds.
cyl: number of cylinders.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
section: Compare fuel efficiency by cylinder group
text:
Compare fuel efficiency by cylinder group
I calculate the number of cars and the average fuel efficiency for each cylinder group.

cylinder_summary <- cars |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_cars = n(),
    average_mpg = mean(mpg),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  cylinder_summary,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Cylinders", "Number of cars", "Average MPG")
)




Cylinders
Number of cars
Average MPG




4
11
26.7


6
7
19.7


8
14
15.1





The four-cylinder cars have the highest average fuel efficiency, at approximately 26.7 MPG. The averages for six-cylinder and eight-cylinder cars are approximately 19.7 and 15.1 MPG.
These are comparisons between the cars in this dataset. They do not show that cylinder count alone explains the differences.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Plot weight against fuel efficiency
I use a scatter plot to check how fuel efficiency changes with car weight. Each point represents one car. I treat cylinder count as a category so each group gets a separate colour.

ggplot(cars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Car weight and fuel efficiency",
    x = "Weight (1,000 pounds)",
    y = "Fuel efficiency (miles per US gallon)",
    colour = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Car weight and fuel efficiency for 32 cars, coloured by cylinder count.





The plot shows a downward pattern: heavier cars generally have lower MPG values. The eight-cylinder cars also tend to appear among the heavier cars with lower fuel efficiency.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Measure the relationship
I calculate the Pearson correlation between weight and MPG.

weight_mpg_correlation <- cor(cars$wt, cars$mpg)

round(weight_mpg_correlation, 3)

[1] -0.868


The correlation is approximately -0.868, indicating a strong negative linear relationship in this dataset.

title: Car weight and fuel efficiency
text:
Conclusion
Heavier cars tend to have lower fuel efficiency in this dataset. Four-cylinder cars also have higher average MPG than the six-cylinder and eight-cylinder groups.
However, this is an observational comparison. Weight, cylinder count, and other car characteristics vary together, so the analysis does not isolate the effect of weight alone.
The data contains only 32 older cars. These results should not be assumed to describe modern vehicles.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text: Do all penguin species have a similar body mass? In this post, I use Python to compare the average body mass of Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. I first check the data, remove records with missing body mass, and then summarize and plot the results.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text: Do all penguin species have a similar body mass? In this post, I use Python to compare the average body mass of Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins. I first check the data, remove records with missing body mass, and then summarize and plot the results.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text:
Data source
I use the Palmer Penguins dataset, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and Palmer Station Antarctica LTER. The data is available under a CC0 licence.
Dataset package citation: Horst, Hill, and Gorman (2020), palmerpenguins.
The Python package includes the data, so this post does not need to download a separate CSV when it runs.

Set up

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

The dataset contains 344 penguins. For this analysis, I focus on the species and body mass columns. Body mass is measured in grams.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text:
Check missing values
Before calculating averages, I check whether any body mass values are missing.

print(penguins[["species", "body_mass_g"]].isna().sum())

penguins_clean = penguins.dropna(subset=["species", "body_mass_g"])

print("Rows remaining:", len(penguins_clean))
print("Rows removed:", len(penguins) - len(penguins_clean))

species        0
body_mass_g    2
dtype: int64
Rows remaining: 342
Rows removed: 2


Two penguins have missing body mass values, leaving 342 records for the comparison. I only remove rows missing values needed for this analysis. Missing values in other columns do not affect this comparison.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text:
Average body mass by species
I group the remaining records by species and calculate the number of penguins and their average body mass.

species_summary = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby("species", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        count=("body_mass_g", "size"),
        mean_body_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean")
    )
    .sort_values("mean_body_mass_g")
)

Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass, at approximately 5,076 grams. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have similar averages, at approximately 3,701 and 3,733 grams.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text:
Compare the averages visually

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

ax.bar(
    species_summary["species"],
    species_summary["mean_body_mass_g"],
    color=["#4477AA", "#228833", "#CCBB44"]
)

ax.set_xlabel("Penguin species")
ax.set_ylabel("Average body mass (g)")
ax.set_title("Average body mass by species")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Average body mass by penguin species, excluding records with missing body mass.

title: Comparing body mass across penguin species
text:
Conclusion
In this dataset, Gentoo penguins have a higher average body mass than the other two species. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have much closer averages.
This comparison only describes group averages. It does not show the variation within each species or account for differences in the proportion of male and female penguins. A useful next step would be to compare body mass by both species and sex.

title: About
text: I grew up in India and spent the last five years working as a data engineer, most recently building a Microsoft Fabric data platform for an agricultural insurance provider in Alberta. Before that I worked with the City of Ottawa and the RCMP, mostly on pipelines, Lakehouses, and the unglamorous plumbing that makes analytics possible. I moved to Vancouver in August 2026 to start MDS.

title: About
text:
Why data science
After years of moving data from one place to another, I kept running into the same wall: I could build the pipeline, but I couldn’t always say what the numbers actually meant. MDS is my attempt to close that gap to get properly fluent in statistics and modelling instead of handing the interesting questions off to someone else. The R half of the program is new territory for me, which is part of the appeal.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
I lift five or six days a week on a push/pull/legs split, and I’m slowly learning which Vancouver trails are worth the drive. I make my coffee at home with a Clever Dripper and a hand grinder, which is either a hobby or a mild compulsion depending on the morning. I also read a fair bit of Indian philosophy, the Gita and the Ramayana and sit for meditation most days.
